lines.text: The market at {name} is audible before it is visible: a specific mix of voices, animals, and the percussion of commerce that no other combination of sounds quite replicates.
{name}'s market day has the comfortable chaos of something that has been happening in the same place for a long time and has worked out most of its problems.
The road into {name} is thick with carts by mid-morning, all of them heading for the same square, and the traffic tells you where the settlement's heart is before you can see it.
You reach {name} against a tide of people leaving it. The market has ended for the day, and the settlement is exhaling its visitors back onto the roads with their purchases and their news.

lines.text: The smell of the river reaches you before the settlement does: clean water, reeds, the particular mud of a working waterfront.
{name} runs along the water the way settlements do when water is the reason they exist: practical, a little chaotic at the waterfront, tidier as you move inland.
The river carries the sounds of {name} to you around the bend before the buildings appear: a mill wheel, the knock of boats against a jetty, someone calling a tally across the water.

{name} has its back to the land and its face to the river; the approach by road brings you in the rear way, past the yards and the drying nets, into a settlement that plainly considers the water its front door.

lines.text: The harbour at {name} announces itself beyond the last rise: masts above the roofs, gulls wheeling over the quays, and salt bright in the air.
{name} faces the sea as deliberately as a fortress faces its enemy. Warehouses and chandlers crowd the waterfront, with the older streets climbing behind them.
You hear {name}'s harbour before you see it: rigging knocking against masts, dock crews calling cargo tallies, and surf working against the outer wall.

lines.text: The sound of a hammer on metal reaches you from {name}'s smithing quarter: a craftsperson's rhythm, not a soldier's.
{name} smells of work: sawdust, tallow, the particular sharp smell of a tanner at the edge of town.
{name} announces its trade before its name: the whine of a lathe, the reek of the dye-vats, a workshop door standing open on a scene of unhurried, practised industry.

lines.text: {name} is ordinary in the best sense: a place where people live and work and argue and sleep, which is most of what places are for.
The road into {name} becomes a street at a point you can't precisely identify. The settlement grows around you gradually.
{name} is neither impressive nor disappointing from the approach. It is what it is, which is a working settlement of reasonable size doing reasonable things.
A child runs past you on the road into {name}, chasing something or being chased by something (unclear which). Nobody in the street pays attention.
A merchant argues with a carter on the road into {name} about the size of a load. Nobody else pays them any attention. This is clearly a daily occurrence.
The first person you meet on the road into {name} wants to know your business, and the second already knows it.
